summary: From prison, John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One; Jesus answers with His works, then honors John before the crowds.
key_insight: Jesus never answers John with a plain yes. He sends back what the messengers have seen, in the language of Isaiah’s promises, with a blessing for anyone not offended by Him. His great praise of John comes only after the messengers have gone.
story: John the Baptist was in prison, and he heard there about the works of Christ. {Mt} Soon after the widow’s son was raised at Nain, John’s disciples told him about all these things. {Lk} So John called two of his disciples and sent them to Jesus with a question: “Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?”
When the men arrived, they repeated John’s words. That very hour Jesus cured many people of infirmities, afflictions and evil spirits, and to many who were blind He gave sight. {Lk}

Then He answered them, “Go and tell John the things you have seen and heard: that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the gospel preached to them. And blessed is he who is not offended because of Me.” {Lk}

As the messengers left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John. “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” A man in soft clothing? Such men live in kings’ palaces. A prophet? “Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet.” John was the messenger of whom it was written, sent to prepare the way. “Among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist; but he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” {Mt}

From the days of John until now, Jesus said, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. All the prophets and the law prophesied until John, “And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come.” {Mt} When the people heard Him, even the tax collectors who had been baptized by John declared God to be right. But the Pharisees and lawyers had refused John’s baptism and “rejected the will of God for themselves.” {Lk}

Then Jesus described His generation. They were like children sitting in the marketplace, calling to their playmates, “We played the flute for you, And you did not dance; We mourned to you, And you did not lament.” {Mt} John came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, {Lk} and they said, “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they said, “Look, a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” “But wisdom is justified by all her children.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew says John heard “in prison” about “the works of Christ.” Luke says John’s disciples reported “all these things,” right after the raising at Nain.
Only Luke says the messengers repeated John’s question word for word, and that in that very hour Jesus healed many and gave sight to many who were blind.

Matthew alone records that the kingdom “suffers violence” and that John “is Elijah who is to come.” Luke alone records how the tax collectors and the Pharisees each responded to John’s baptism (7:29–30).
Matthew says there “has not risen one greater” than John; Luke says there is “not a greater prophet.” Matthew ends, “wisdom is justified by her children”; Luke, “by all her children.”

scene.label: John in prison
scene.text: Herod Antipas had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife (Matthew 14:3–4). The Jewish historian Josephus names the place: Machaerus, Herod’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

scene.label: “The Coming One”
scene.text: John had preached about “He who is coming after me” (Matthew 3:11). The phrase pointed to the promised Messiah, the one who comes in the name of the Lord (Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1).

scene.label: Isaiah’s signs
scene.text: Jesus’ list echoes Isaiah: the eyes of the blind opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, the lame leaping (Isaiah 35:5–6), and good tidings preached to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). John knew these promises well.

scene.label: Reeds and soft clothing
scene.text: Tall reeds grew thick along the Jordan, where John baptized, and bent with every gust. Fine clothes belonged in palaces like Herod’s. John wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (Matthew 3:4). He was neither a waverer nor a courtier.

scene.label: Games in the square
scene.text: Children in the town square played at weddings with flutes and at funerals with wailing. Jesus pictures children who sulk and will join neither game: John was too stern for them, and Jesus too friendly with sinners.

witnesses.matthew: Places the question at the start of chapters 11–12, where Israel’s responses to Jesus begin to divide. Matthew calls Jesus’ deeds “the works of Christ” and alone records Jesus naming John as the promised Elijah, the forerunner of Malachi 4:5.
witnesses.luke: Sets the question right after Jesus raises the widow’s son at Nain, so “the dead are raised” had just happened. Luke alone shows the crowd dividing over John’s baptism, and he follows at once with a meal where a sinful woman shows what “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” really means.

seeing.reveals: Jesus does not scold John for asking. He answers a faithful servant’s doubt with evidence and with Scripture, and then, when John’s men are gone, honors him as more than a prophet.
seeing.living: John’s question came from a prison cell, where the Messiah he had announced was not doing what he expected. Take that kind of question to Jesus Himself, as John did, and weigh His answer by His works and by the Scriptures. His blessing rests on the one who keeps trusting Him when His ways are not what we pictured.
seeing.ponder: Where has Jesus not acted the way you expected, and is that becoming a reason to stumble, or a reason to look again at what He has done?

preaching.big_idea: When Jesus does not meet our expectations, He is still fulfilling every promise of God.
outline: An honest question from a prison (18–20)
An answer from the works and the Word (21–23)
A tribute to the faithful forerunner (24–28)
A generation that refused every call (29–35)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus answers in the words of Isaiah 35:5–6 and 61:1, the very prophecies John knew. The only personal word He sends back is a beatitude (v. 23), a gentle warning wrapped in a blessing.
